extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and science journalists tracking retractions and misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: Identify criteria and signals that lead journals or institutions to issue expressions of concern, corrections, or retractions (especially in biomedical research). Includes institutional investigation outcomes, ethical lapses, and data/image problems cited in retraction reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guilty of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional finding that authors committed scientific misconduct (e.g., Karolinska declared Paolo Macchiarini and co-authors 'guilty of misconduct').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as grounds for journals to retract papers after receiving requests from institutions; exemplified by The Lancet retracting papers 'after receiving requests to do so from the new President of the Karolinska Institute (KI)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of Concern (EOC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal issues an expression of concern to alert readers when questions about a paper cannot be resolved immediately (e.g., JCS issued an EOC while KI investigated concerns about Fig. 1A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EOCs are used when the journal has received a tip/concern and refers the matter to the authors' institution or cannot resolve the issue internally; can be updated or removed depending on institutional findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional request for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: An institution (university/ethical review board) requests that a journal retract a paper following its own investigation (e.g., KI contacting journals to request retraction after investigating Macchiarini papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may act on formal requests from institutions; institutional determinations carry weight in subsequent editorial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship removal / disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may ask to have their names removed from papers (e.g., a co-author asked to be removed from Macchiarini’s Lancet paper), indicating serious disagreements about the content or conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author removals can signal underlying misconduct or disputes and often prompt further scrutiny, corrections, or editorial notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of IRB / ethical approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to follow proper ethical procedures such as lacking institutional review board (IRB) approval or other required oversight (noted in cases where researchers 'didn't follow proper ethical procedures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly salient in clinical or human-tissue research; absence of required approvals can form a basis for investigations, corrections, or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image duplication or manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicated or manipulated figures/images in papers (e.g., inadvertent figure duplication cited in a 2011 paper; Oncogene retraction prompted by image duplication concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image problems can lead first to corrections, then to expressions of concern or retractions if additional issues surface or cannot be resolved; often detected by readers or on platforms like PubPeer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections that fail to resolve issues (correction → retraction pathway)
rubrics_metrics.description: A published correction may later be followed by a full retraction if readers raise additional questions about the corrected material (example: a paper corrected in 2016 was later retracted when further concerns arose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections do not always settle concerns; persistent or new questions after a correction can escalate to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable findings / unreliable data
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings judged unreliable (category tags such as 'unreliable findings' applied to posts), forming a reason for expressions of concern or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreliability may be due to methodological, data, or ethical problems and is cited as a basis for retraction or editorial notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower and reader complaints as triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints from whistleblowers, co-authors, or readers (e.g., whistleblowers filed complaints against Macchiarini; readers alerted journals to image/data concerns) trigger investigations and editorial actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External tips commonly initiate journal inquiries or institutional investigations that can result in EOCs, corrections, or retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical review board determinations and calls for multiple retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert or central ethical review boards may review multiple papers and call for retraction when concerns are justified (example: Central Ethical Review Board called for six retractions relating to Macchiarini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal determinations from ethics bodies can lead to coordinated requests to journals and broader scrutiny across a researcher’s body of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical / human-subject misconduct in experimental treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct specific to clinical or experimental treatments (e.g., experimental trachea transplants and use of unapproved procedures leading to patient harm and later misconduct findings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical misconduct encompasses failing to follow ethical/consent procedures, experimental treatment improprieties, and patient-safety issues; such cases often attract institutional inquiry and public editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal publisher notes and updates following institutional conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may append publisher’s notes or update prior EOCs/corrections based on the outcomes of institutional investigations (example: JCS updated an expression of concern after KI concluded its investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial records (publisher’s notes, updated EOCs) document how journal responses evolve as new institutional information becomes available.
